title: POC Weekly - Dedicated Burst Policy Ops Sync
summary: Weekly POC sync to review last week's burst rehearsal results, tune autoscaling policies for Dedicated cluster, reconcile latency vs cost tradeoffs, and align on next benchmark and security deliverables.
topics: SOC2 audit docs and KMS questions
action_items: Ivy Zhang — run 2nd burst run using policy: min_replicas=2, max_replicas=12, scale_by=queue_length; capture per-GPU util and 95pct latency (due: 2026-12-20)
Samir Patel — provide realistic 5-minute traffic trace (CSV) including diurnal spikes and examples of 1-second spike (due: 2026-12-18)
Marco Ruiz — share Dedicated pricing worksheet and estimated prewarm costs for warm pool of 3 GPUs (due: 2026-12-17)
Tom Wu — confirm KMS rotation policy requirement and whether HSM is mandatory for PII keys (due: 2026-12-22)
Liam Carter — schedule follow-up deep-dive with SEs to review kernel selection logs and KV cache hit rate (due: 2026-12-21)
next_steps: Ivy to re-run burst with queue-based scaling and attach raw logs + csv metrics to this thread
Customer to send traffic trace and test accounts for replay
Redwood to produce warm pool cost estimate and recommended autoscale cooldowns
Schedule security call to walk through SOC2 artefacts and KMS integration (Tom + Marco + Redwood Security)
Follow-up meeting 2026-12-22 at 14:00 UTC for results review
transcript:
Header: Date: 2026-12-15, Time: 14:00 UTC, Duration: ~47 minutes, Attendees: Liam, Ivy, Marco (Redwood); Nora, Samir, Ana, Tom, Jae-min (GreenShift).
[00:00] Liam (Redwood AE): All right folks, thanks for joining. we'll go quick — agenda is readout from last week's burst rehearsal, policy tuning, cost implications, and security Qs. Nora, anything to add?
[00:22] Nora - GreenShift: No, that's good. we wanted to focus on the high-latency tails we saw during the 90-second spike and figure out whether prewarming or more aggressive scaling is better.
[00:33] Ivy (Redwood SE): Yeah, quick recap — last Thursday we ran the 5x spike sim against your Dedicated pool: baseline 45 rps steady, we ramped to ~620 concurrent requests over about 90 seconds. we logged scheduler decisions, GPU util, and kv-cache hit rates.
[00:50] Samir - GreenShift: kv cache? I saw something about K V cash in the notes, is that your cache for transformer states?
[00:57] Ivy: sorry yeah, KV cache — occasional transcription of notes — it's the key-value decoder cache. hit rates were around 78% for the short prompt flows, dropped to 53% when we hit a lot of cold-start flows.
[01:14] Ana - SRE: That 53 percent seems low, are we sure it's not the replay harness sending slightly different prompt prefixes?
[01:21] Ivy: Good call. Samir, your harness samples did include randomized user prefixes; that reduced reusability. For the burst run we can fix that to measure the best-case reuse.
[01:33] Marco (CSM): I'll also point out we saw a lot of queueing for the head node for about 30 seconds while autoscaler spun up new replicas.
[01:40] Tom - Security: On my side, still waiting to know how keys are stored in Redwood private — KMS vs HSM. does the POC on Dedicated use customer-managed keys?
[01:51] Liam: For this POC we've been using Redwood-managed KMS for convenience, but the Dedicated product supports customer KMS via AWS KMS or cloud HSMs for Private deployments. We'll get you the docs.
[02:04] Jae-min - Data Sci: Quick question — what model variant were you using during the run? FP16 quant or int8?
[02:11] Ivy: We used a 16-bit quantized variant (FP16) with some operator fusion enabled. We haven't pushed int8 for this particular model because of small quality regressions we wanted to avoid during POC.
[02:22] Nora: Ok, can you summarize the latency numbers one more time? the product team needs a short blurb for execs.
[02:29] Ivy: Sure — baseline traffic: 45 rps, median per-response latency ~210ms, p95 about 480ms during steady-state. During the 90s spike, with default scaling (min=1,max=8,cooldown=60s, scale_by_cpu), p95 climbed to ~1.8s and we observed about 8-10s tail cases caused by queueing and cold starts.
[02:49] Samir: Hmm 8-10s tails is not great. Did we try prewarming?
[02:53] Ivy: We ran a small prewarm of 2 GPUs which helped reduce the worst tails to about 3-4s, but cost went up ~18% for the window. There's a tradeoff.
[03:06] Nora: What about warm pools or keep-alive instances?
[03:09] Ivy: Warm pool of 3 GPUs would keep model weights resident and eliminate many cold init costs; our estimate is around $X/day for 3 GPUs in your Dedicated footprint — Marco will share exact numbers.
[03:20] Marco: Yup I'll post the pricing sheet. also note we have a warm-pool abstraction now that can be sized separate from autoscale so you can keep N instances resident and let autoscaler add more.
[03:31] Ana: On networking — during the spike we saw a few TCP connection resets in the VPC logs. could that be the head node overloaded?
[03:38] Ivy: Possibly, or it could be ephemeral ENI limits in your account. We saw bursts in packet drops correlating with the moment the autoscaler started attaching instances. We'll need to check VPC quotas and MTU settings.
[03:52] Tom: Also curious about audit logs — when we spin up replicas, what logs are available for compliance purposes?
[03:58] Liam: We surface audit logs for control plane actions, model loading events, instance lifecycles; for Private deployments we can ship full host-level logs into your SIEM. We'll share SOC2 artefacts.
[04:12] [04:12] Nora: Great. Ivy, what's the recommended autoscale policy change to reduce the 95th percentile without exploding cost?
[04:18] Ivy: Two levers: switch the scaler to queue_length (requests waiting) with a low threshold, and reduce cooldowns to 20s to let replicas come up faster. Add a warm-pool of 2-3 GPUs to absorb the first wave. Also tune target_concurrency per replica down slightly so each GPU accepts fewer concurrent chains which reduces tail latency.
[04:38] Samir: If we reduce target_concurrency, we'll need more replicas for same throughput, cost goes up though.
[04:44] Ivy: Correct, that's the tradeoff. Another approach is to enable continuous batching with lower batching max time to keep tokens moving — that'll help throughput without proportionally more GPUs.
[04:56] Jae-min: Any quality regressions from changing concurrency? We worry about beam search deterministic behavior — will that change output ordering?
[05:03] Ivy: No, concurrency per replica is orthogonal to decoding behavior; it's about how many independent requests share the device. Decoding remains deterministic per request.
[05:11] Marco: We also logged kernel selection anomalies; some sequence length distributions caused a non-optimal kernel being chosen and spiking GPU mem copies which added ~100-200ms overhead. We'll include those logs.
[05:26] Samir: Can we force a specific kernel or quant profile?
[05:29] Ivy: You can pin a quantization profile per model version or set a preferred kernel tag, but we usually recommend letting the runtime pick the best for the observed distribution. For the POC we can try a pinned config to measure differences.
[05:40] [05:40] Nora: Let's dial in an action plan — what should we test next run?
[05:45] Liam: Ivy, propose concrete test matrix.
[05:47] Ivy: Proposal: three runs — A) queue-based scaling, min_replicas=2, max=12, cooldown=20s, warm_pool=2; B) same but with warm_pool=0 and prewarm 2 GPUs at spike start; C) increased target_concurrency with continuous batching tweaks to see cost trade offs. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 latencies, GPU util, KV-cache hit rate, and scheduler events.
[06:12] Ana: That sounds good. Also please log socket metrics so we can correlate the resets.
[06:17] Ivy: Will do.
[06:19] Tom: Security question: during scaling, are model artifacts pulled from your object storage or from a local cache? concern is exfil during startup.
[06:28] Ivy: Models are pulled from the internal artifact store during initial load unless you pin models into a customer-provided object store for Private. For Dedicated we can support S3 with fine-grained IAM roles; download happens over TLS. We'll document the flow.
[06:41] Jae-min: On metrics — can we get per-token cost breakdown? We want to attribute cost to embeddings vs debate vs gen.
[06:48] Marco: Our Console provides token-level cost by route and model. For POC I'll attach a sample export.
[06:55] [06:55] Samir: A practical question on cooldowns — 20s seems aggressive; aren't you worried about flapping?
[07:02] Ivy: Good point. You want a short cooldown to react quickly to spikes but combine with scale stabilization logic: e.g., require N consecutive intervals over threshold before scaling down. That avoids flapping.
[07:15] Nora: Ok. We also need to know the expected lead time for warm pool allocation — is it instantaneous?
[07:22] Ivy: Warm pool instances are pre-initialized; adding them is usually <10s because model weights are resident. Starting new replica cold is longer — depends on model size, often 15-40s.
[07:33] Ana: In our logs we saw one replica take ~56 seconds to be ready, is that within normal?
[07:39] Ivy: That's high — might be network or an instance throttling event. We'll check kernel logs and node provisioning logs for that timestamp.
[07:49] Tom: If we go to Private on-prem later, are these timings similar?
[07:54] Liam: On-prem timings depend on your hardware and storage; typically less network variability but you may still have model load times unless you keep a local cache.
[08:03] [08:03] Nora: Any blockers from Redwood for the next run?
[08:07] Ivy: We just need your synthetic traffic trace (Samir) and permission to enable queue-based scaler and warm-pool on the trial cluster. Also we need to push slightly different kernel pins for run B.
[08:19] Samir: I'll get the trace by Friday.
[08:22] Marco: I'll send the pricing and the warm-pool cost estimate by tomorrow.
[08:27] Tom: For SOC2 docs — can you provide your latest report and a list of encryption-at-rest controls?
[08:33] Liam: Yep, Marco will kick that off.
[08:37] [08:37] Nora: Anything else?
[08:39] Jae-min: Small note — please include the prompt buckets used in the run so we can reproduce model-quality signals.
[08:45] Ivy: We'll attach the prompt buckets.
[08:48] [08:48] Ana: Onburst mitigation — have you experimented with request shaping (client-side) to smooth spikes while autoscaler catches up?
[08:56] Ivy: Yes, request shaping on the client side (smoothing) plus a reasonable warm pool often gives the best latency/cost balance. We can recommend a small client-side token-bucket limiter for bursty clients.
[09:08] Samir: Ok we'll test that too.
[09:10] Liam: Great — let's recap next steps and owners. Ivy will run the three test runs and produce raw logs; Samir provides traffic trace; Marco sends pricing and SOC2 artefacts; Tom to confirm KMS/HSM needs. We'll reconvene next Tuesday.
[09:26] Nora: Thanks everyone.
[09:28] Liam: Thanks, we'll follow up in the thread with the run configs. Bye.
[09:32] [END]
